items.summary_original: Blender Foundation and the online community proudly present Blender 5.3 ! Blender 5.3 splash artwork by Blender Studio , featuring a scene from the OVERGROWN teaser . Download this .blend file What’s new Blender 5.3 wraps up 2026 with new features and improvements across the board. The headliner is native support for 3D Gaussian Splats . You can import them from PLY and SPZ files as point clouds, to then edit and process them with Geometry Nodes, relight and render in Workbench, EEVEE and Cycles. Asset Libraries can now be shared as extensions, and the Extensions platform accepts Asset Libraries containing Public Domain (CC0) assets. The Outliner now finally allows users to arrange objects freely with custom sorting. On NVIDIA GPUs, a new DLSS denoiser for the viewport gives a cleane

items.title: Send the Firefighters to the Fires
items.summary_original: Send the firefighters to the fires Enterprise software keeps forgetting a century of good advice about what deserves our attention. House fire in New Zealand neighborhood If a user’s job is to fix what’s broken, the screen should show what’s broken first. Sounds pretty obvious. It’s also not new. Frederick Taylor argued for it in 1903. Xerox PARC designed for it in the ’90s. Industrial control rooms wrote it into a standard. Yet enterprise software keeps forgetting this. Imagine a fire department that dispatches trucks in the order houses were built. Or by date last renovated. Every house gets a visit eventually, and some of them happen to be on fire. That’s pretty absurd, right? Yet I’ve seen the equivalent more times than I care to remember. A lot of enterprise work boils down to one job

items.title: NIKE rethinks air cushioning with digitally printed patterns inside its soles
items.summary_original: NIKE TUNED AIR CHANGES HOW SNEAKER SOLES ARE BUILT NIKE has found another use for ink, and this time it has little to do with logos or graphics. The company has introduced Tuned Air, a manufacturing process that uses digitally applied ink to determine how different sections of an air-filled sole behave under pressure. Presented on November 16, 2026, the technology changes the internal construction of NIKE's familiar Air units rather than introducing an entirely new cushioning material. The idea is to control which areas compress, which remain firmer and how the sole responds to movement. Traditional NIKE Air units rely on internal pins and rigid sections to maintain their shape, a construction method that also limits how their geometry can be adjusted. items.title: interview: meeting the soft, breathing creatures of katrijn westland
items.summary_original: Westland makes textiles that move and respond Katrijn Westland’s Soft Companions brings together knitted textiles , natural dyes, sensors, and pneumatic systems to create a collection of creature-like objects that breathe, move, emit warmth, and respond to touch. Developed through the Dutch designer’s background in scenography and interaction design, the project considers what happens when design stops looking at materials as passive objects and treats them as entities with behaviors that invite human attention and care. Westland creates an ecology of sensory-responsive companions that invite us to reconsider how we relate to the material world. Her interest in this relationship starts with textiles. We are in constant contact with them, through the clothes we wear and the fabrics we touch

items.title: »Man kann Kreativität nicht auf ein einziges Modell beschränken«

items.title: Typography as Spacial Intervention
items.summary_original: Directed and designed by Paula Minelgaitė, HOCA3 investigates a sharp, cross-disciplinary question: how urban design operates as a graphic expression in physical space, and conversely, how typography can function as a literal spatial intervention on the page through concrete poetry. The resulting compositions completely challenge traditional readability paradigms. You will find a highly limited, pragmatic use of color paired with raw abstraction, striking geometry, and different typefaces thrown together in varying, unpredictable scales in non-traditional compositions. Text is deployed as a visual art form, forcing the viewer to navigate the page the same way an inhabitant navigates a complex, non-linear city street. Built entirely outside the traditional academic and commercial publishing

items.title: MECCHA KIREI. GRAPHIC DESIGN IN JAPAN
items.summary_original: What does contemporary graphic design in Japan look like through the eyes of a younger generation? How have environmental, health, and nuclear crises shaped their practices, and what role do women play in the Japanese design field? Based on field research and interviews conducted since 2018, Alexandre Dimos takes a closer look at around twenty Japanese graphic designers born between 1970 and 1990. The book explores their work, careers, and the role they play in graphic design today. When looking at Japanese graphic design from a Western perspective, only a few names have become widely known, including Tadanori Yokoo and Ikko Tanaka. Since World War II, independent designers and advertising agencies have shared commissions, with many of their works accompanying Japan’s economic development

items.title: Studio Kiln builds a shape-shifting character for weight loss app Reset
items.summary_original: Meet Ester, who's made of tumbling blocks and sits at the heart of a warmer, less preachy identity. Sadly, the terms 'weight-loss app' and 'empathy' don't naturally go together. Typically, such apps feel more like a nagging aunt: counting every calorie, logging every slip, basically doing everything but calling you an overweight loser. Reset wants to do things differently. First launched in 2019, this app is aimed at those who'd rather not count every calorie and want to progress at their own pace. It begins by calculating your metabolic type, then adapts its guidance accordingly. To better convey that approach, Reset turned to Studio Kiln, the design studio founded in Falmouth and now splitting its time between Cornwall and London, as we explored in this interview a couple of months back.

items.title: Gutes Leben. By Design: Was Gestaltung kann, zeigt der neue Auftritt des IDZ
items.summary_original: Das Internationale Design Zentrum Berlin (IDZ) positioniert sich neu. Und das mit einem Erscheinungsbild des Studio Peter Post × Petra Esveld, im kräftigen Orange, mit einem besonderen Z – und als starkes Statement, welche Wirkkraft Design hat. Seit 1968 engagiert sich das Internationale Design Zentrum Berlin (IDZ) dafür, die Wirkmacht von Design sichtbar zu machen. Das unterstreichen nicht nur der Bundespreis Ecodesign oder die UX Design Awards, die es vergibt, sondern vor allem auch die kontinuierliche Arbeit des IDZ, Gestalter:innen mit Wirtschaft, Forschung und Politik zu vernetzen. Und das jetzt mit einem neuen Erscheinungsbild, das vom Studio Peter Post × Petra Esveld gestaltet wurde – und jede Menge Fragen stellt. Allen voran die provokante: Verchromt Design die Misere? Und auch »Mu

items.title: rune bosse puts living trees on life support in a vision of ecological collapse
items.summary_original: rune bosse's lung trees imagine a forest on life support Danish artist Rune Bosse places living trees on artificial life support in Lung Trees, an installation presented at the Danish Architecture Center in Copenhagen as part of its Age of Nature exhibition, which ran through September 2026. Each tree stands inside a transparent, inflated plastic enclosure, and is surrounded by mechanical equipment and artificial lighting. With their branches reaching toward overhead lamps, each tree seems to have been removed from the forest and placed under intensive care. The installation imagines a future in which trees might depend on technology to survive, even as humans continue to depend on the ecological systems that trees help sustain. It reverses a relationship we tend to take for granted. Fores
items.title_de: Rune Bosse setzt in einer Vision eines ökologischen Zusammenbruchs lebende Bäume auf Lebenserhaltung
items.summary_de: Die Lungenbäume von Rune Bosse stellen sich einen lebenserhaltenden Wald vor Der dänische Künstler Rune Bosse setzt lebende Bäume auf künstliche Lebenserhaltung in „Lung Trees“, einer Installation, die im Dänischen Architekturzentrum in Kopenhagen im Rahmen der Ausstellung „Age of Nature“ präsentiert wird, die bis September 2026 lief. Jeder Baum steht in einem transparenten, aufgeblasenen Kunststoffgehäuse und ist von mechanischer Ausrüstung und künstlicher Beleuchtung umgeben. Da ihre Äste bis zu den Deckenlampen reichen, scheint es, als ob jeder Baum aus dem Wald entfernt und auf die Intensivstation gebracht worden wäre. Die Installation stellt sich eine Zukunft vor, in der Bäume zum Überleben auf Technologie angewiesen sein könnten, während die Menschen weiterhin auf die Ökosysteme angewiesen sind, die Bäume unterstützen. Es kehrt eine Beziehung um, die wir normalerweise für selbstverständlich halten. Fores
